lesson.title: Telophase: Two Nuclei, Almost Two Cells
lesson.summary: Telophase is the final stage of mitosis, when the two separated sets of chromosomes decondense and are enclosed in newly reformed nuclear envelopes, essentially reversing prophase as the cell prepares to split in two.
lesson.body:
Telophase is the final stage of mitosis, and in many ways it is prophase running in reverse. The two full sets of chromosomes, now gathered at opposite poles of the cell after their journey through anaphase, begin to decondense, unwinding from their tightly packed mitotic form back into the loose chromatin state suited for gene expression. Around each decondensing set, a new nuclear envelope reassembles, built from fragments of the original envelope and from pieces of the cell's membrane system, and the nucleolus reappears inside each newly formed nucleus. The spindle microtubules, having finished their job of separating the chromosomes, disassemble.

By the end of telophase, the cell has two separate, fully reformed nuclei, each containing one complete copy of the genome, sitting inside what is still, at this exact moment, a single cell. Splitting that one cell into two happens through cytokinesis, which usually starts during the later part of anaphase or telophase and finishes shortly after. In animal cells, this is carried out by the contractile ring introduced earlier, a band of actin microfilaments that tightens around the cell's midline like a drawstring, pinching it into two separate cells along a crease called the cleavage furrow. Plant cells, which have a rigid cell wall, divide differently, building a new cell wall structure between the two nuclei instead of pinching the membrane inward, though the underlying goal is the same.

Once cytokinesis completes, the result is two separate daughter cells, each with its own nucleus, its own full set of chromosomes, and its own complement of organelles and cytoplasm. Each of these new cells now enters G1 of a fresh cell cycle, ready either to grow and divide again or to exit into the quiescent G0 state, closing the loop back to where the cell cycle overview began.
